title: The example of the wise (3.17–3.29)
hook: people copy what you do, not what you say, and Krishna says even he keeps working for that reason

segments.voice: Yesterday, yajna — the wheel of sacrifice: food, rain, offering, action, and the one who only takes. Your line was give back. What did you hand on? Today, who's watching you turn the wheel. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

If you've ever been around a small child for more than a day, you know. They don't do what you tell them. They do what you do. You say be gentle, and then you slam the cupboard, and guess which one they learn. The same is true in offices, teams, families, whole countries. People watch the person at the front, and they copy. Krishna has just told Arjuna to work as an offering. Now he adds a reason Arjuna hadn't thought of. Even if you didn't need to act, other people need you to.
screen: `THEY DO WHAT YOU DO.` → `PEOPLE WATCH THE ONE IN FRONT.` → `OTHERS NEED YOU TO ACT.`

segments.voice: Krishna begins with the rare person who's already free: someone who delights in the self, is content in the self, has nothing left they need to do. You'd think that person could stop. But, Krishna says, look at King Janaka. Janaka was a ruler famous for his wisdom, a sage who never left his throne, and he and others like him reached perfection through action. Then the word for why: lokasangraham evapi sampashyan kartum arhasi. Keeping in view the holding-together of the world, you should act. Lokasangraha: the good of the world, the keeping of people together. Then the famous line. Yad yad acharati shreshthas tat tad evetaro janah. Whatever the best person does, others do the same. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. And here Krishna points at himself. There's nothing in all three worlds I have to do, he says, nothing I lack and need to get. And yet I keep acting. Because if I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So, he says, the wise should act as eagerly as the attached do, but unattached, for the good of the world. And they shouldn't unsettle simpler people who are attached to their work; they should do the work well beside them. One more turn at the end. All actions are carried out by the qualities of nature, the gunas. Only the one confused by ego thinks, I am the doer: ahankara vimudhatma kartaham iti manyate. The wise lead by example, and they don't take the credit.
screen: `JANAKA: A SAGE WHO KEPT HIS THRONE.` · `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLD THE WORLD TOGETHER.` · `WHATEVER THE BEST DO, OTHERS DO.` · `EVEN KRISHNA KEEPS WORKING.` · then, large: `LEAD BY DOING, NOT BY TAKING CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see who's watching. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people who see you most: a child, a younger sibling, a coworker, a friend who's struggling, even a stranger on your usual bus. Let their faces come one by one. Now ask, gently: if they copied exactly what I did yesterday, not what I said, what would they learn? Don't judge it. Just see it. Then pick one small thing you'd be glad for them to copy, and picture yourself doing it in front of them tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Lokasangraha. The good of the world, the holding-together of people. Whatever the best person does, others do the same, so even the free keep working, for the good of the world.
Your line: lead by doing. Today, do the thing you keep telling other people to do, where they can see it, and don't mention it. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often cite Gita 3.20–3.21, on lokasangraha and on people following the example of the best, when speaking of leadership, parenting and public service, and King Janaka is remembered as the model of a wise person who kept working in the world.

original.note: Sanskrit: loka, the world, and sangraha, holding together. the good of the world, in Gita 3.20.

trapdoor: what you thought: set a good example.
what it means: people copy what the best do, so even the free keep working, for the world's sake, without thinking I am the doer.
what a scholar hears: lokasangraha, 'holding the world together', became a key word for modern Hindu thinkers of public service, from Tilak to Gandhi.
